title: Explaining the second line: a feeling you must join
summary: New Orleans music is a feeling; you have to participate, and funeral second lines celebrate after mourning.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: How do you explain to someone who has no idea about the second line — I mean for instance I’ve only seen it on film. And sometimes I’m not sure what that is really all about.

Right. And you know I said this yesterday, speaking about my friend Mark Roe, who said to me once that New Orleans music is a feeling. And he is exactly right. And I think about the city that way. And so I was trying to convey that yesterday when I was speaking to the audience, is that I can try to explain it to you, but I know that I really can’t explain it to you. You have to participate in it. That’s what this music and the city is all about. You have to become engaged in it. And what I find is that I usually, I mostly feel that, I find that people come to New Orleans and they either love it — extremely love it — or they hate it and they feel like it’s the worst place on earth. Now of course everybody is entitled to their own opinion. So that what I always say, come to New Orleans. Come to the Treme and join a second line and feel that and hang out and find yourself two miles from where you started and stopping at a bar here and a bar there and having a drink and friends, and yeah.
You have to let go of your inhibitions, don’t you? To do that?

Yeah. I think so. I think the music is a lot about that, letting go of inhibitions. They have second line parades after funerals. And so — to celebrate peoples’ lives. You know, it’s a celebratory time as well as a mournful time. And the celebration comes after the mourning. But you’re letting go of everything, and you’re just feeling how great it is. But of course that’s individual. It’s an individual thing but it’s a collection thing too, obviously, because you get swept up by things sometimes. It’s such a movement.
